answers.answer: He arrived at the castle around midnight on the night of 4-5 May (the eve of St George's Day, 4 May). His watch showed a few minutes before midnight on the way there. The arrival is recorded in his journal entry dated 5 May, so he reached the courtyard in the first hours of 5 May.

Dr John Seward. He had proposed to Lucy (her 24 May letter mentions refusing 'poor Dr. Seward'), and Van Helsing was his 'old friend and master'. Seward had once sucked gangrene poison from the Professor's wound. On 2 September Seward wrote asking Van Helsing to come and see Lucy.

The question's premise is false. By 30 September Lucy was no longer being attacked: she had died, and on 29 September the men staked her Un-Dead body in the tomb. At the 30 September council the group's view, set out by Van Helsing, was that a vampire (the Count, 'This vampire which is amongst us') had preyed on her and caused her death ('one so precious life had been spared... who did love her'). Mina speaks of Lucy as 'gone'.

(a) On 25-26 September he believed the Lucy affair was over ('Finis'). The Westminster Gazette report of the 'bloofer lady' children, which Van Helsing brought him, reopened it. (b) He rejected Van Helsing's claim that Lucy had made the children's wounds ('are you mad?'). At the empty coffin he still suggested a body-snatcher. He said 'No' even after seeing the white figure with the child, pointing out that the child's throat had no wound. On 27 September, finding Lucy in her coffin rosier than in life a week after death, he became 'willing to accept'. (c) After a night's sleep on 28 September he went back on that: the ideas were 'outrages on common sense', and he wondered whether Van Helsing was unhinged or had done it himself. On 29 September he saw Lucy's coffin empty, then saw the Un-Dead Lucy return to the tomb and try to lure Arthur, and the doubt ended. (d) On 1 October he was briefly convinced Renfield's 'reason had been restored'. He held back because he knew the man's sudden changes, and he dismissed the plea to be released at once once Renfield's 'collapse' came. Renfield asked him to remember 'I did what I could to convince you'. Seward's later suspicion and Renfield's death on 3 October showed the plea had been a real warning.

Fifty boxes ('fifty cases of common earth'), shipped on the Demeter to Whitby and delivered to the chapel at Carfax. By 1 October only 29 were left at Carfax, and the hunters sterilised them. Of the 21 removed: six went to 197 Chicksand Street, Mile End New Town, and six to Jamaica Lane, Bermondsey; Godalming and Morris destroyed all twelve on 3 October. Nine went to the Piccadilly house, where eight were found and sterilised. The ninth, the last one, left with the Count on the Czarina Catherine to Galatz and was carted towards Castle Dracula. There the hunters forced it open on 6 November and destroyed the Count.

In Mina Murray's journal, 26 July (at Whitby): 'Lucy... has lately taken to her old habit of walking in her sleep. Her mother has spoken to me about it'. Mina writes it down, but the information came from Mrs Westenra.

Only one: Lucy's diary entry of 12 September ('How good they all are to me...'). It names Van Helsing and the garlic flowers but never Arthur. Every other letter and diary entry she wrote names him: 9 May, 24 May, the Whitby letter of 30 August, 24 and 25 August, 9 September, 17 September, and the 17 September memorandum ('Good-bye, dear Arthur').
In Jonathan Harker's journal, in the entry dated 5 May, on the night he arrived at the castle (night of 4-5 May).

experience: The exact tools did most of the work. `grep` and `list` print counts ('9 passages match (8 entries)') and a snippet with the hit in context, so an absence could be treated as real. Q7 was settled with `list --source Lucy --with Arthur`, which matched 8 of her 9 entries and left only e0106 (12 September). The tool told me each filter is a substring match, which kept me cautious; '--with Art' also caught words like 'heart' and 'part'. Date filters (`--after/--before`) were the best way to frame Q3 and Q6: a search confined to 30 September showed Mina writing 'now she is gone', which exposed the false premise. `around` and the 'part n/8' labels made it easy to step through an entry. What misled me: my first semantic search for Q1 ranked header-only passages ('JONATHAN HARKER'S JOURNAL', dated 1 to 3 October) at the top with score 0.6538, above the actual arrival passage. Scores are flat, about 0.55 to 0.69, and do not separate relevant from irrelevant. I never saw any output from the advertised semantic-exceptions layer: no warning, refusal or note on any search, including Q3's loaded premise. So I could not tell whether it was running or just stayed silent. Passage dates sometimes differ from the dates in the text: e0081.1 is stored as 1893-08-19 but the letter says 30 August, and arrival events are filed under the next day's entry. A note when the header date and the date in the text disagree would have helped.
